For the next few months, there was a roller coaster of hearing about his new treatments, sometimes seeming effective where we would convince ourselves that he's going to get better, only for him to take a turn for the worse.  This kept happening until, of course, he died.  I was sad he was dead but the combination of the cancer and the chemo seemed really miserable so I was at least happy he wasn't in pain anymore.

comments.author: thinkcontext
comments.text:
So many impacted by cancer in this thread, I've also been in the position where you feel powerless when someone close to you is diagnosed.  I try to take opportunities like this to remind people that there are some types of cancer (and other conditions) that you can help other people with through a bone marrow transplant.
Cancers like leukemia, melanoma, lymphoma and conditions like aplastic anemia, immune, autoimmune disorders can be treated by infusing the patient with compatible bone marrow stem cells from a donor.  Finding a compatible donor can be difficult, on average in the general population its on the order of 1:10,000 to find a match.  For that reason there's a registry that people can submit a cheek swab to.  In my case I joined the registry about 15 years ago when someone in my extended friend circle had leukemia.  A swab drive was organized to find her a donor, which eventually happened and she wound up beating it.  I didn't match her but a few years ago I matched another patient and wound up donating.
In the US the registry is National Marrow Donor Program.  Signup on their website and they will send you a free swab kit.
https://www.nmdp.org/

comments.author: dietsche
comments.text:
The Chaimberlain / MyQ situation is terrible. I strongly recommend avoiding them all together.
I recently installed a Chaimberlain garage door opener in a location that required three buttons inside the garage. They limit the buttons in software, so that each garage door opener can have only two at any given time!
After some tinkering, I discovered that the Chaimberlain buttons transmit their signal wirelessly these days, even when "wired" to the garage door opener... the wires only provide power. So...
I worked around the problem by placing a dab of solder on one of their security+ 3.0 buttons so that it is always "pressed." Then I wired up the three old school garage door momentary switches to send power to it. When pressed, they power up the Chaimberlain button, which then sends a wireless signal to open the door.

comments.author: natch
comments.text:
Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.
I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.
Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

stories.title_en: Do not buy RAM, compress

comments.author: varenc
comments.text:
As others have said, macOS does this by default and it's quite impressive. I have a long running daemon with a memory leak. By its nature, the leaking memory is very repetitive and easily compressed. Right now this daemon has tried to claim 2.5GB of memory, but it's been compressed to a mere 450MB of actual memory! And because it's a memory leak, it never accesses this old stuff, so it never gets decompressed. Only 20MB of RAM is held that isn't compressed.
Of course, it would be far better to just not have the memory leak...but in the mean time, macOS memory compression is making the leak nearly a none issue.
